title: Promoting ESA Software as a European Product: The SCOS-2000 Example
short_title: Promoting ESA software: the SCOS-2000 example
organisation: European Space Agency, ESOC (Directorate of Technical and Operational Support; Directorate of Industrial Matters and Technology Programmes)
status_notes: Published magazine article (bulletin 108, november 2001, printed pages 72-77).
summary:
An ESA Bulletin article (November 2001) by J-F. Kaufeler and M. Jones of ESOC's Ground Segment Engineering Department and H-U. Karl of the ESOC Contracts Service on the initiative to promote SCOS-2000 as a supported ESA software product, not only as licensed in-house software.

It explains why ESOC bases every mission's control system on one generic system and lists the four strategic aims of SCOS-2000: ease of configuration, functional richness, scalability and vendor independence. It gives history and numbers: work started in about 1992, the first missions (Huygens, Meteosat MTP LEOP and Teamsat) were supported in 1997, the telecommanding chain was re-engineered in 1998-2000, about 15 MEuro had been invested, and control-system costs fell by a factor of two to three. It describes the port from Solaris to Linux and the replacement of the commercial ObjectStore and Orbix by the open-source POST++ and Omniorb, with ILOGViews kept for the user interface for now.

Much of the article is about licensing: ESA's 'operational software' IPR clause, free non-exclusive licences to Member State bodies, the three licence types (run-time, development, full), and a move towards open-source-style terms under which licensees hand back kernel improvements. It compares SCOS-2000 with US commercial products, lists the support set up (user organisation, FTP documentation server, help desk), and reports early results: the first users workshop (April 2001), adoption by DLR's German Space Operations Centre, use by the Herschel/Planck payload teams for instrument checkout (checkout changes pioneered on Proba), about 30 licences, and plans for certification and a Windows port.

It documents why and how SCOS-2000 spread beyond ESOC, including into EGSE.

contents.title: Introduction and ESOC software products and their marketing
Licensing aspects: the current ESA licensing scheme

key_points.text: ESOC has used a generic mission control system as the basis for each mission's control system for over 25 years; SCOS-2000 is its latest generic system.

SCOS-2000 strategic aims: ease of configuration/customisation, functional richness, scalability and vendor independence; all four were achieved and ESOC control-system costs came down by a factor of between two and three.

Work on SCOS started in about 1992; its first ESA missions, Huygens, Meteosat (MTP) LEOP and Teamsat, were supported in 1997; the telecommanding chain was re-engineered in 1998-2000; total investment was of the order of 15 MEuro.
SCOS-2000 originally ran on Sun Solaris; it was modified to run under Linux, and of its three COTS products (ObjectStore, Orbix, ILOGViews) the first two were replaced by POST++ and Omniorb.
SCOS-2000 was to be used for all future ESA missions, for example Rosetta, which extends up to 2013.

ESOC uses three licence types: run-time licences (temporary use and trial), development licences (upgrades of operational software under ESA contract) and full licences (developments based on the software).
The main competing products came from US suppliers such as Integral Systems, Storm and Braxton Technologies.
Nearly 100 people from outside ESA attended the first SCOS-2000 Users Workshop in April 2001.

DLR's German Space Operations Centre chose SCOS-2000 for its control centre infrastructure, and the Herschel Planck payload PIs chose it for their instrument checkout equipment; checkout support was pioneered for Proba and introduced into the evolution version.
Some 30 SCOS-2000 licences were granted in a little over two years, making it the best-selling product licensed through ESOC's Contracts Service.
A certification activity with the ESA Quality Department was starting, using a method customised from ISO 9126 and developed with TUV Cologne; a study showed a Windows port to be feasible.
From ESOC alone, 93 software products had been licensed in 94 Member State bodies, with more than 220 licences in total.
